---
title: "OPDI Papers"
---

Methodology studies behind the [Open Performance Data Initiative](https://www.eurocontrol.int/opdi).

Each paper benchmarks an OPDI algorithm against EUROCONTROL reference data and
reports what the comparison actually showed, including where a proposed method
failed.

Older papers render from a committed CSV cache — no credentials, no database, no
cluster. **The current papers render by running their analysis**: every figure
is produced by a job that declares the source files it depends on, so a figure
and the code that made it cannot drift apart. That costs cluster access to
re-render a stale page, which is the intended trade. ADEP/ADES versions 1–6 and
flight events versions 1–2 pre-date the change.

## Papers

:::: {.publication-card}
::: {.publication-info}
**[ADS-C in the OPDI trajectory — version 1](adsc-fusion-v1/index.qmd)**
&nbsp;·&nbsp; [PDF](adsc-fusion-v1/adsc-fusion-v1.pdf)

Tests whether merging OpenSky's ADS-C feed into the ADS-B trajectories improves
flight-event extraction. ADS-C is merged **before** segmentation, so `track_id`
sees both sources, and the trajectory cleaner is made source-aware — its
twenty-second isolated-point rule would otherwise delete a feed whose median
cadence is several hundred seconds, and the fusion would have measured as a
no-op for a reason unrelated to its idea. Both arms are rebuilt from the same
state vectors and scored against APDF over the twenty aerodromes of flight
events version 4.

Reports what the feed actually is, measured over eleven days spanning 2023-09
to 2026-10: a few thousand rows a day inside OPDI's European box, almost all
above FL300, most of them west of 10°W, no `on_ground` flag ever true, and
every speed, temperature, wind, selected-altitude, registration and type field
empty on **every** day sampled. The A-CDM runway family therefore cannot move,
and that null is reported as measured rather than omitted.

Also measures what the two feeds disagree about. They agree on where the track
is to within a few metres across track and disagree by hundreds of metres along
it — a timing offset, not a position error — and that offset is a property of
the individual airframe, not of the feed. One aircraft in twenty-five is
persistently about thirteen seconds out while another is synchronised to a
hundredth of a second, which is why no global correction is applied.

**Pending its data campaign.** The page renders against
`benchmarks/regenerate_adsc_v1.py`; where a figure is not yet staged the table
says so in place, and the provenance chapter lists what is present.
:::
::::

**[Flight events from ADS-B — version 4](flight-events-v4/index.qmd)**
&nbsp;·&nbsp; [PDF](flight-events-v4/flight-events-v4.pdf)

Supersedes version 3. Replaces `ATOT`/`ALDT` — shown in v3 to be the extreme
sample of a detection window, not a measured instant — with nine A-CDM
milestones (line-up, take-off-roll, airborne, landing, touchdown,
runway-vacated, go-around and two runway-crossing types) derived from one
explicitly classified runway traversal, with the three instants among them
interpolated to the geometry that defines them rather than sampled near it.
Moves the vertical profile to EUROCONTROL PRU's published methodology, and
closes two silent unit defects where the airport-layout gate and the
level-segment floors were compared against uncorrected pressure altitude.

**Pending its benchmark campaign.** The page renders against
`benchmarks/regenerate_events_v4.py`; where a figure is not yet staged the
table says so in place rather than being omitted, and the provenance chapter
lists what is present.
:::
::::

:::: {.publication-card}
::: {.publication-info}
**[Flight events from ADS-B — version 3](flight-events-v3/index.qmd)**
&nbsp;·&nbsp; [PDF](flight-events-v3/flight-events-v3.pdf)

The one to read. Audits the four detectors behind OPDI's published flight
events, which had never been tested or compared against reference data, finds
nine defects — one of which means no take-off or landing has ever been emitted
for any aerodrome above roughly 200 ft — and adds the milestone families the
ICAO GANP indicators require, taking the reachable KPI count to nine fully and
three partially computable.

Version 3 is organised as **one chapter per event**. Each says what the event
is, how it is detected, which parameters govern it, how it changed from the
published algorithm, and whether any external source agrees with it — or why
none can. It closes three comparisons that had been coded and never run: ring
crossings against EUROCONTROL's own, runway identity against `AP_C_RWY`, and
the inter-source floor that says what "close" can mean. **The ring crossings
land inside that floor** — the detector agrees with the reference about as
closely as the reference agrees with itself.

A closing chapter designs a parameter sweep — what to optimise, against what
objective, at what cost, and which values must not be touched — without running
one.

States plainly what it has *not* measured, and reports two of its own fixes
that the data contradicted.
:::

**[Turning ADS-B state vectors into flight tracks — version 5](track-construction-v5/index.qmd)**
&nbsp;·&nbsp; [PDF](track-construction-v5/track-construction-v5.pdf)

Makes `cruise_linked` the default track rule. A flight that loses reception for
over 30 minutes keeps one `track_id` when the data either side of the gap fits one
continuous flight: flights crossing the edge of the European box come out in one
track 81.5% of the time against 25.3% before, with 1 false join in 5,888
checkable linked gaps. Fixes what version 4 left open: level segments and
flight-level crossings no longer span a gap, cumulative distance reads the last
known position (a defect that had left every track 14% short), and the flight
list names the aerodrome it actually ranked first. An independent audit found the
linking decisions sound and one read-window defect in the callsign guard, fixed.
A descending new edge now links too: the three false joins that kept it off were
estimated arrival times outside Europe, and the study's truth no longer counts
those. One pipeline day shows nothing else moved: 15,032 tracks identical under
both rules give identical airports and events. The page and PDF are built from
the CSVs, not yet rendered with Quarto.
:::
::::

:::: {.publication-card}
::: {.publication-info}
**[Turning ADS-B state vectors into flight tracks — version 4](track-construction-v4/index.qmd)**
&nbsp;·&nbsp; [PDF](track-construction-v4/track-construction-v4.pdf)

A flight crossing the Atlantic loses reception for hours, and any gap over 30
minutes ends its track, so one flight becomes two rows with neither airport pair
whole. A new rule, `cruise_linked`, keeps one `track_id` across a hole when the
evidence at its edges fits one continuous flight: flights crossing the European
box in one track rise from 25.3% to 80.7%, with 3 false joins in 5,773 checkable
holes and 6 of 123,949 artificial gaps hiding a real landing joined. Edge values
read past blank samples, and an old edge still climbing can link, provisionally,
on 185 checkable holes; a new edge descending stays split. About three in four
linked holes cannot be checked, because truth is European. Does not recommend
making it the default yet: level segments span a hole on most linked tracks,
cumulative distance runs short across one, and promotion would add another silent
`track_id` boundary. Superseded by version 5, which fixes both, audits the rule
and makes it the default; frozen as the record of the proposal.
:::
::::

:::: {.publication-card}
::: {.publication-info}
**[Turning ADS-B state vectors into flight tracks — version 3](track-construction-v3/index.qmd)**
&nbsp;·&nbsp; [PDF](track-construction-v3/track-construction-v3.pdf)

A defect in the rule version 2 shipped, found after the fact: the break fires
on a callsign change but never asks whether the callsign changes back. A
flicker — a callsign decoded wrong for one sample and then right again —
trips the break twice, trisecting a flight that never changed. 23.1% of every
track boundary the shipped rule draws on a sample day traces to a flicker leg,
against 5.0% that are a genuine change. The fix, `debounced`, requires a new
callsign to persist before it counts: about 19% fewer tracks, a
persisted-callsign guard that shrinks rather than grows as the hold
lengthens, and no measured increase in genuine two-flight fusions. States
plainly what APDF's block times cannot referee here — rounding and
transponder dwell put timing out of reach — and uses movement counts as a
guard instead, which passes. The fix ships in the codebase and defaults off;
promoting it would break `track_id` continuity a second time, which this page
declines to decide on its own.
:::
::::

:::: {.publication-card}
::: {.publication-info}
**[Turning ADS-B state vectors into flight tracks — version 2](track-construction-v2/index.qmd)**
&nbsp;·&nbsp; [PDF](track-construction-v2/track-construction-v2.pdf)

The release note for the segmentation version 1 recommended, and the answer to
the question version 1 could not ask of itself. Version 1 scored candidate
rules in a harness reading a track table someone else had built; this runs
three of them through the real pipeline — ingestion, track building, cleaning
and the flight list — and reports what the shipped code does. The finding
holds: the recommended rule beats the published one by about 40 points of
one-to-one matching in the harness and about 40 in the pipeline, so the result
was not an artefact of the harness. Separates the two changes that produced it,
finding the airframe-only grouping worth most of the gain and the
callsign-change break worth the last two points and most of the merging.

Also the operational warning. **No `track_id` survives this release.** The
published rule suffixes `_{year}_{month}` and the new one an offset, over
different grouping keys, so not one identifier carries across — by
construction, not by measurement — and the track count falls by about a third.
Anything joining on `track_id` across the boundary gets nothing.
:::
::::

:::: {.publication-card}
::: {.publication-info}
**[Turning ADS-B state vectors into flight tracks — version 1](track-construction-v1/index.qmd)**
&nbsp;·&nbsp; [PDF](track-construction-v1/track-construction-v1.pdf)

The segmentation question underneath every other paper on this page: which
state vectors belong to the same flight, decided once and inherited by
everything downstream — the flight list groups by `track_id`, events are
extracted per track, measurements accumulate from a track's start. Finds that
the rule behind every `track_id` OPDI has published to date recovers only
about half of flights one-to-one, and that a full sweep of its three
thresholds barely moves that number — the cause is the grouping key,
`(icao24, callsign)`, which starts a new track whenever a callsign is decoded
blank. Grouping on the airframe alone and splitting only on a genuine
callsign change closes most of the gap, and is worth an order of magnitude
more than the parameter sweep found. Documents a labelling bug in
`flights.py` that the switch exposed — a blank callsign sorted first, which
was harmless only while every track carried exactly one — and that had to be
fixed before the better segmentation could ship without making the published
flight list worse.

Scores every rule over two intervals: the airborne leg, and gate to gate. The
second is what the first cannot see — a rule carrying callsign in its grouping
key loses fourteen to eighteen points once the stand and the taxiways count,
because a callsign goes blank or rotates while the aircraft is parked, and the
airborne interval never looks there. Eleven minutes of the median flight sit
outside it. Chapter 7 sweeps the shipped rule's own thresholds rather than the
retired one's, and finds the shipped values within 0.18 points of the best cell
of 235 — while the best cell on one sample is beaten by the shipped values on
the other, which is why nothing was retuned.
:::
::::

**[Departure and destination aerodromes in the OPDI flight list — version 7](adep-ades-detection-v7/index.qmd)**
&nbsp;·&nbsp; [PDF](adep-ades-detection-v7/adep-ades-detection-v7.pdf)

**The one to read if you use the data.** Written for people consuming the `ADEP`
and `ADES` columns rather than for the people building them: what they mean, how
the pipeline derives them from raw ADS-B, how often they are right, and what a
downstream analysis should do about the failure modes.

Documents the pipeline end to end for the first time, and measures every change
on two independent periods — which is what showed that three values version 6
shipped were not supported, and got them changed. Departures and arrivals use
different algorithms; candidates are chosen by exact distance rather than a
hexagon index; and a departure's null now separates "outside the observed area"
from "could not tell".
:::
::::

:::: {.publication-card}
::: {.publication-info}
**[Detecting departure and destination aerodromes from ADS-B — version 6](adep-ades-detection-v6/index.qmd)**
&nbsp;·&nbsp; [PDF](adep-ades-detection-v6/adep-ades-detection-v6.pdf)

The consolidated study. Re-measures every sweep against the pipeline as it now
stands — no number is carried over from earlier versions — and settles what
production should run. Finds that the algorithm already in service was never
tuned: its flight-level gate was fixed at FL40 and never swept, and moving it is
worth thousands of correctly named flights per three-day sample. Departures and
arrivals turn out to want different algorithms.

Written as a working record rather than for an outside reader; version 7 is the
one to send to someone who will *use* the flight list.
:::
::::

:::: {.publication-card}
::: {.publication-info}
**[Detecting departure and destination aerodromes from ADS-B — version 6.2](adep-ades-detection-v6.2/index.qmd)**
&nbsp;·&nbsp; [PDF](adep-ades-detection-v6.2/adep-ades-detection-v6.2.pdf)

Combines the version 6 and 6.1 reports and adds one change: `trend`'s
altitude cut now measures height above the aerodrome's own field elevation
rather than sea level, matching every other altitude test in the pipeline —
`endpoint`'s, step 04's ground phase. The aggregate effect is close to
nothing by construction, since most arrivals sit at aerodromes below 500 ft
where the two datums are identical either way, but the gain lands exactly
where elevation predicts it should. Restates the standing conclusion:
departures want `endpoint`, arrivals want `trend`, and choosing among
candidates by exact great-circle distance rather than H3 ring count is worth
more than any threshold on the page.
:::
::::

:::: {.publication-card}
::: {.publication-info}
**[Reply to the review of version 6](adep-ades-detection-v6/reply.qmd)**
&nbsp;·&nbsp; [PDF](adep-ades-detection-v6/reply.pdf)

Answers a review of version 6 point by point, in the reviewer's order, with the
numbers computed from the same committed data the review was about. Confirms
three things the review suspected and one it did not: the flight-level curve
does turn rather than rising indefinitely, the arrival tuning does hold on a
second period once the two are ranked together, `trend` genuinely could not say
"out of area" — and trajectory cleaning, step 02a of the pipeline, had been
writing a table that nothing read.

Deliberately pinned to the figures that were reviewed. Where an answer changed
once the measurements came in — out-of-area was built and then left off — the
page says so rather than being quietly revised.
:::
::::

:::: {.publication-card}
::: {.publication-info}
**[Detecting departure and destination aerodromes from ADS-B — version 5](adep-ades-detection-v5/index.qmd)**
&nbsp;·&nbsp; [PDF](adep-ades-detection-v5/adep-ades-detection-v5.pdf)

Takes the arrival deficit apart. Finds it is silence rather than error, that
most of that silence is the abstention refusing candidates it is right to
refuse, and that a bearing test — does the trajectory point at the aerodrome? —
is the first signal to beat it. Establishes why: a position difference survives
the archive's carried-forward staleness, and a rate does not, which is why
vertical rate, closing rate and the approach cone all failed.
:::
::::

:::: {.publication-card}
::: {.publication-info}
**[Thinning state vectors, and what the archive actually contains](statevector-decimation/index.qmd)**
&nbsp;·&nbsp; [PDF](statevector-decimation/statevector-decimation.pdf)

Tests whether OPDI's 5 s decimation rule — a fixed-phase `event_time % 5`
filter — loses data where reception is intermittent. It does not: the OpenSky
archive is a complete 1 Hz grid, and a correct bin-based sampler recovers 0.22%
more rows. The experiment instead finds that the grid is padded with
carried-forward positions, and that the staleness is wildly asymmetric — a
departure's first fix is fresh, while an arrival's last fix carries a position
measured a median of 190 seconds earlier.
:::
::::

:::: {.publication-card}
::: {.publication-info}
**[Detecting departure and destination aerodromes from ADS-B — version 4.5](adep-ades-detection-v4/index.qmd)**
&nbsp;·&nbsp; [PDF](adep-ades-detection-v4/adep-ades-detection-v4.pdf)

Moves detection into the OPDI pipeline itself: H3 cells as the index, exact
great-circle distance as the comparison, three modes behind one parameter.
Finds that the detection radius barely matters for coverage while the height
threshold decides almost everything — but that read on accuracy the two axes
pull the other way, so a coverage-only view overstates the case for a high
threshold. The production baseline improves enough under the new candidate
stage to overturn version 3's conclusion. Breaks results down by class of
aerodrome, which shows the method answering small aerodromes and heliports
confidently and wrongly every time. Explains the preprocessing pipeline, each
mode, and every metric from first principles.
:::
::::

:::: {.publication-card}
::: {.publication-info}
**[Detecting departure and destination aerodromes from ADS-B — version 3](adep-ades-detection-v3/index.qmd)**
&nbsp;·&nbsp; [PDF](adep-ades-detection-v3/adep-ades-detection-v3.pdf)

Finds that six of the seven most frequent departure errors were a scheduled
civil airport losing to an adjacent military airfield, and removes that class
entirely with a scheduled-service preference. Fixes an out-of-area rule that was
pre-empting valid aerodrome matches, reports out-of-area recall and precision
separately for the first time, and carries a production patch proposal for
`flights.py`.
:::
::::

:::: {.publication-card}
::: {.publication-info}
**[Detecting departure and destination aerodromes from ADS-B — version 2](adep-ades-detection-v2/index.qmd)**
&nbsp;·&nbsp; [PDF](adep-ades-detection-v2/adep-ades-detection-v2.pdf)

Corrects two accounting errors in version 1. A large share of flights have an
origin or destination outside the ingested area, and scoring those as detection
failures understated every method; and the aircraft filter was an allowlist
that discarded 47.74% of the fleet to exclude the 8.64% that are rotorcraft.
Adds trajectory extrapolation (which fails), the cleaning ablation, the
aerodrome-set sweep, an error breakdown, and a measurement of `track_id`
quality.
:::
::::

:::: {.publication-card}
::: {.publication-info}
**[Detecting departure and destination aerodromes from ADS-B — version 1](adep-ades-detection/index.qmd)**
&nbsp;·&nbsp; [PDF](adep-ades-detection/adep-ades-detection.pdf)

A comparison of seven ADEP/ADES methodologies against APDF ground truth over
two three-day samples a year apart. Finds that the production algorithm's
altitude-trend logic contributes no accuracy over a nearest-aerodrome rule on
the same flights, and that replacing it with explicit endpoint abstention
improves departure detection by 8–10 points of coverage — while the same
change fails to replicate for arrivals, and is not claimed.
:::
